            subject of the representation difficult to identify (figs. 6.7 and 6.11). Among
            Holm’s most important findings was the identification of the three design
            units that are the building blocks of Northwest Coast compositions, the
            “ovoid” (a slightly squared-off oval with a concave bottom contour), the
            “U-form,” and the “formline.” An artist’s equipment included sets of different-
            sized templates of ovoids and U-forms which he traced onto the design field
            without prior sketches but with such precision that the spaces between the
            main design units emerge as a continuous flowing line, termed by Holm the
            “primary form line” (fig. 6.8). This line lies on the surface plane and
            is almost always painted black in two-dimensional compositions. It is a




06-Berlo-Chap06.indd 215                                                                                                                            22/05/14 5:11 PM
    216     |    T he North w est C oa st


                                flowing contour whose width widens and narrows as it changes direction
                                and encounters other lines. Subsidiary design areas are linked by a red “sec-
                                ondary formline,” and a third infilling of negative spaces between the two
                                formlines may be added and painted blue or blue-green. The tertiary lines
                                are often carved out in shallow relief. Research by Bill McLennan also shows
                                that a great deal of painting was done freehand.15 Holm concluded that,
                                even when an artist was making a three-dimensional object, such as a box,
                                a spoon handle, or a totem pole, he first conceived of the design in two di-
                                mensions and then mentally “wrapped” it around the three-dimensional
                                surface before carving it out in relief. It is particularly easy to visualize this
                                process in relation to the design of decorated bowls and boxes used for
                                feasts and for storing important possessions, which constitute one of the
                                most important genres of Northwest Coast art. A box is constructed from a
                                single plank into which wedge-shaped cuts, or kerfs, are made where the
                                corners will occur. The plank is then steamed, bent at right angles, and sewn
                                with spruce root along the open edge. In formline-style art, the two sides of a
                                being may be d  ­ isplayed on opposite sides of a bowl or a box, or laid out as
                                mirror images on a flat surface ­according to a characteristic convention
                                known as “split representation” (fig. 6.22, far right).
                                   The monotony that might result from the strict limitations that the
                                formline style imposes on practitioners (who were, up until the twentieth
                                century, men) is avoided by a number of other design strategies also iden-
                                tified by Holm. For example, although compositions are largely symmetri-
                                cal, the Northwest Coast artist characteristically avoids both absolutely
                                parallel lines and true concentricity in the placement of ovoids and other
                                forms. He also calibrates nicely the curving shapes of his design units and
                                formlines to fall between the e­ xtremes of angularity and curvilinearity.
                                The formline style is a highly ­d isciplined mode of graphic representation
                                that eliminates all extraneous elements. Yet it also lends itself to subtle
                                invention and variation. The hands of individual artists can be detected by
                                attending to such details as the ­precise degree of off-centeredness with
                                which the artist avoids an exact concentricity in the placement of the
                                pupil within the eyeball, or in the subtle differences in the ways in which
                                each artist proportions and contours his U-forms, ovoids, and formlines.
                                The study of individual artists’ styles is an area of expanding research
                                among Northwest Coast artist and scholars.16 Building on Bill Holm’s
                                work, Peter Macnair, Robin Wright, Bill McLennan, and Lyle Wilson have
                                made signal contributions, clarifying the bodies of work that can be at-
                                tributed to artists active in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centu-
                                ries such as Charles and Isabella Edenshaw (see Artists in Focus box),
                                Simeon Stilthda (ca. 1799–1889), John Gwaytihl (ca. 1820–1912),
                                Tom Price (ca. 1860–1927), John Robson (1846–1924), Willie ­Seaweed
                                (1873–1967), and Charlie James (1870–1956).
                                   The limited number of basic design units also gives rise to a characteris-
                                tic representational feature of Northwest Coast art. Because the same or
                                similar design units are used for different body parts—a U-form for a fin
                                or a tail, an ovoid for an eye or joint—the style lends itself to the creation
                                of visual puns in which a particular form can be read simultaneously as

            part of two different, overlapping images. Northwest Coast artists have
            exploited this capacity to the full, using it to play on fundamental philo-
            sophical perceptions of structural dualities, the deceptiveness of appear-
            ances, mythic processes of transformation, and the paradoxical coexistence
            of two truths at a single juncture of time and space.17 The contemporary
            Haida artist Robert Davidson speaks of the explorations of fundamental
            cosmological principles that occur in the working out of formline composi-
            tions. He has described, for example, his conversations with apprentices
            while creating an important housefront painting: “All the time we were
            working on it, I stressed the importance of space, how one line relates to
            another line, or how the ovoid related to the U-shape, or how the ovoid re-
            lates to the space around it, and I talked about the balance, and how fragile
            things were”18 (fig. 7.24).
               The earliest objects that can firmly be identified as coming from the
            Kwakwaka’wakw and Nuxalk of the central coast were collected in the mid-
            nineteenth century, and these show an extensive use of the conventions of
            the formline style. Yet archaeological evidence suggests that the arts of the
            central province were formerly more like those of other Wakashan speakers
            such as the Nuu-chah-nulth. In two-dimensional painted designs this “ar-
            chaic” style, which is still evident in Coast Salish and Nuu-chah-nulth art,
            displays tendencies toward elegant simplifications of form that can verge on
            abstraction (fig. 6.9). In many three-dimensional objects, this art displays
            more angular transitions of plane and a tendency to flatness that contrasts
            with the deeper relief characteristic of more northerly carving traditions.
            Although ovoids and U-forms are present in southern province art, their use
            is more limited and they tend to be realized as more regular geometric forms.
            Other characteristic linear motifs, such as crescent and “T” shapes, are, how-
            ever, important design ­elements, incised into surfaces to define facial fea-
            tures and limbs and used decoratively in repeated groupings (fig. 6.5). In his
            analysis of northern coastal arts, Holm also identified “slits” and “resultant
            forms” that occur in between the main design units as important

                                      northern style was spreading south, aided both by long-standing customs of
                                      commissioning works of art to be made by well-known artists from neigh-
                                      boring tribes and by more recent increases in intertribal marriages involving
                                      transfers of crests, ceremonial privileges, and art treasures. The process of
                                      stylistic transfer, however, was far from mere copying; it generated new
                                      styles with their own unique features. In contrast to Haida or Tlingit art, for
                                      example, Kwakwaka’wakw carving of the second half of the nineteenth cen-
                                      tury is ­renowned for its more organic, fully sculptural volumes, its bold but
                                      less s­ ystematic use of formline design, and its bright polychrome surfaces
                                      which make lavish use not only of the red, black, and blue-green of the north
                                      but also of white, yellow, cobalt, and green (fig. 6.10).


                                      Western Connoisseurship and Northwest Coast Art
                                      As we have seen, research reveals the formline style to be a local development
                                      within a broader stylistic complex, albeit one of great refinement and aesthetic
                                      power. Yet it has had a disproportionate profile in the literature on Northwest
                                      Coast art that can be compared to the dominance of Florentine art in the
                                      literature on the early Italian Renaissance or the art of the Classic Maya in
                                      ancient Mesoamerica. Moreover, art collectors’ appreciation of the relative
                                      naturalism and refinement of the Northern style is evidenced by the prices
                                      realized at auction for such objects (fig. 6.14). This privileging of the northern
                                      style has led to a tendency to discuss Northwest Coast arts in terms of center
                                      and margins and reflects Western rather than Indigenous perspectives on
                                      quality and aesthetics. In a 1930 monograph on the Coast Salish, for example,
                                      Erna Gunther and Hermann Haeberlin stated: “The Puget Sound people repre-
                                      sent a very marginal development in the art of wood working, having essen-
                                      tially the forms used to the north, but none of the artistic finish or even fine

            highly sophisticated art style,” he reversed the ­earlier ­pronouncements of
             Gunther and Haeberlin.25
                Comparative judgments of the importance of an art tradition are also
            ­influenced by a gendered and hierarchical Western classification of artistic
             media. If textile traditions, rather than carving, are taken as a measure of
             the degree of artistic development, then the southern coastal peoples would
             be regarded as equally accomplished. The colorful, geometric blankets of
             mountain-goat wool woven by Coast Salish peoples during the nineteenth
             century and revived toward the end of the ­twentieth, for example, rival those
             of the Navajo in color and pattern (figs. 6.13 and 2.23).
                Moreover, two of the most important and iconographically elaborated
             types of Salish wood carvings—spindle whorls and mat creasers—are im-
             plements used in weaving. To be drawn into such comparisons, however, is
             precisely to fall into the trap we should seek to avoid. Visual arts are related
             both to the distinctive historical exchanges that have occurred over time in
             a given area and also to the contexts of expression that are important in
             that place. The remainder of this chapter underlines this general point by
             looking at a series of contexts that promote the production of visual art on
             the Northwest Coast, and illustrates them through examples of particular
             regional traditions in which these contexts are especially important.

      OBJECT IN FOCUS
      A Tsimshian Mask and Questions of Patrimony

      The Northwest Coast is a region rich in
      masking traditions. Each region has pro-
      duced its own mask types in distinctive
      styles ranging from the refined natural-
      ism of the northern coast to the bold,
      colorful, and theatrical masks of the cen-
      tral coast and the planar geometries of
      the southern peoples. The Tsimshian are
      northern peoples; although the name
      means “people of the Skeena River,”
      today it refers to those whose homelands
      are at the mouth of the river, where, as
      archaeological studies show, they have
      lived for more than 5,000 years.
          In 1863, the year after the devastating
      smallpox ­   epidemic reached northern
      British Columbia, Scottish ­        minister
      Robert Dundas visited the Anglican mis-

      Rupert. The resident missionary William
      Duncan gave his visitor seventy-seven tra-
      ditional ceremonial objects surrendered
      by those who had converted to Christian-
      ity. As Karen Duffek has remarked, “It
      was an exchange of the carved manifesta-
      tions of clan histories for the promise of
      more powerful cosmologies—and access
      to new economies—during a period of

            Contexts for Art: Power, Status,
            and Cross-Cultural Exchange
            Shamanism
            Shamanism, as noted in chapter 1, is a system of religious practice in which
            an individual enters into a trance state in order to contact other-than-­
            human spirits. In many societies specialist shamans use their connections
            to powerful helper spirits on behalf of community members for healing,
            controlling weather, locating animals, or success in warfare. As Esther
            Pasztory has pointed out, visual arts of high aesthetic quality are not essen-
            tial to the efficacy of shamanistic practice.28 Drums and rattles, for exam-
            ple, which are used by shamans around the world to induce a trance state
            and to summon spirit helpers, are most often undecorated. Two Northwest
            Coast art traditions, the Straits Salish and the Tlingit, are not only excep-
            tions to this general pattern but also provide two contrasting examples of
            the use of visual art in shamanistic practice.
               Among the Straits Salish of Puget Sound, visual aids are used not only by
            shaman-specialists, but by ordinary people in the tending of the individual
            guardian spirits they acquire through vision quests. The forms of the visual
            “props” made by both are similar, although they are used in different rituals
            and for different purposes. As in the Plains and Woodlands, people tradi-
            tionally acquire guardian spirits during puberty seclusion, and these bestow
            abilities, such as exceptional skill in basketry or in the hunting of certain
            animals. An individual’s guardian spirit is traditionally believed to travel
            around the world each year. Its annual return at the time of the winter cer-
            emonial season causes its owner to fall ill, and friends and family gather to
            restore health by helping him or her perform the spirit’s songs and dances.
            In the nineteenth century, these spirit dances were the central events of the
            winter ceremonials, and participants wore elaborately beaded clothing and
            headdresses. In the Soul Recovery Ceremony, which is more properly trans-
            lated as “Spirits-Curing-in-a-Line,” a group of shamans made use of special

                               of shamans journeyed into the underworld to recover the lost soul whose
                               absence caused the patient’s illness. The house was mystically transformed,
                               in part with painted boards representing spirits encountered on the voyage,
                               which were sometimes arranged to demarcate the shape of a canoe. Such
                               visual aids were not created to be permanent works of art. Rather, because
                               of the potentially dangerous spirit power they contained, they could be used
                               only once before being discarded. Visual art in this context was a secondary
                               adjunct to the singing that is the central focus of the ritual.29
                                  Among the Tlingit, as among the Coast Salish, specialist shamans used
                               their extraordinary powers of communication with the spirit world for
                               ­healing. They also conducted important rituals on behalf of the community,
                                such as the annual First Salmon Ceremony, a ritual intended to influence
                                the return of the salmon to village fishing grounds. Nowhere else on the

                                     constructive and sanctioned; the chief, for example, exercises his powers and
                                     control over food resources on behalf of his dependents, while the shaman
                                     heals or ­communicates with animals to help the hunter.

            Crest Art
            As we have seen, the building blocks of Northwest Coast style are the indi-
            vidual design units described earlier, while many important individual icono-
            graphic motifs appear to be derived from shamanistic concepts of power. The
            larger and more familiar units of visual art, especially on the northern and
            central coast, are the more complex images of humans and animals known as
            crests. Crests are often compared to the heraldic devices displayed by aristo-
            cratic European families on their coats of arms, a comparison which has
            merit for a number of reasons. Both coats of arms and crests are exclusive
            designs that can only be used by their rightful owners, powerful families who
            control land and resources. As in European heraldry, too, Northwest Coast
            families usually own more than one crest image, acquired over the genera-
            tions through marriage or conquest in war. Through shared crests, families
            recognize different levels of relationship. Some peoples, too, are subdivided
            into two large subdivisions, or moieties, such as the Haida eagle and raven, or
            into several clans, such as the Tsimshian eagle, raven, wolf, and killer whale.
            A family’s crests include those of the moiety or clan as well as those it owns
            individually, and no two families will possess exactly the same set of crests.
            Finally, as with European coats of arms, crests are displayed on a Northwest
            Coast family’s house, on the canoes in which its members travel (today for
            ceremonial purposes), and on a wide range of other possessions as a way of
            advertising the status and identity of family members.
               The most famous and dramatic mode of crest display is the crest or
            “totem” pole, a tall pillar of cedar that can reach a height of 60 feet.33 Halpin
            identified five distinct kinds of crest poles serving specific architectural and
            functional purposes: (1) interior house posts that support roof beams;

                                       (2) house frontal poles placed along the central axis of the outside façade
                                       and often containing an opening used as a ceremonial entrance; (3) memo-
                                       rial or commemorative poles, usually erected by the successor to a title in
                                       order to commemorate his predecessor; (4) welcome figures, placed on the
                                       beachfront to greet visitors; and (5) mortuary poles, made to support grave
                                       boxes usually placed in front of a house. As previously noted, it is likely that
                                       crest poles became larger and more numerous during the nineteenth cen-
                                       tury because of the increased wealth, competitiveness, and access to metal
                                       tools that resulted from European contact. The fronts of Northwest Coast
                                       houses were built in a line along river or sea shores. During the second half
                                       of the nineteenth century the dense rows of housefronts, soaring poles, and
                                       painted crest designs ornamenting many villages became a favorite subject
                                       for photographers (fig. 6.19). In the late nineteenth century, with the popu-
                                       larity of tourist boat journeys up the Inside Passage to Alaska, the totem
                                       pole, as Aldona Jonaitis and Aaron Glass have shown, came to rival the
                                       feathered war bonnet as a continent-wide symbol of “Indianness.”34
                                          The analogy between Northwest Coast crests and European heraldry tells
                                       only a part of the story of the meaning of crests. When a Tsimshian chief
                                       recounts his Adaawk (oral history), he is at the same time claiming a complex
                                       of interde­pendent possessions: crests, names, titles of ­chieftaincy, rights to
                                       dwell in a certain house, stories, songs, dances, and visual images, as well as
                                       rights to certain lands, fishing areas, and hunting grounds. On one level, the
                                       crest ­explains how all these things were initially bestowed by nonhuman
                                       beings in the early time of the world, when humans and animals could more
                                       easily pass in and out of each other’s domains. The stories often celebrate
                                       the daring and courage of an ancestor who was able to enter the other
                                       domain and bring home rewards still ­enjoyed by his or her descendants.




06-Berlo-Chap06.indd 228                                                                                             22/05/14 5:12 PM

            To depict these encounters, artists use devices such as visual punning and
            split representation to give concrete form to the notions of transforma-
            tion, fluidity, and doubled reality that characterize primordial time.
                  The story of the Dog-Salmon Pole from the Gitksan village of Gitwangak
            (Kitwanga) on the Skeena River illustrates the way this system of visual
            images and oral traditions works (fig. 6.20). Because the crest poles at
            ­Gitwangak have been much studied by ethnographers, their imagery is
             ­unusually well documented. (For the majority of poles now in public collec-
              tions, the detailed stories have been lost, although individual beings can
              often be identified. This loss is a direct result of the removal of these poles
              from communities where such knowledge can be transmitted transgenera-
              tionally.) The Dog-Salmon Pole honors Tewalas, a great warrior and
              ­fisherman, and commemorates his encounter with the Dog-Salmon. In
               1925 the name Tewalas belonged to a woman, Mrs. Augustus Sampere—a
               not unusual occurrence, for many Northwest Coast peoples have systems
               either of matrilineal, ambilineal, or bilateral descent. Harlan Smith ­recorded
               one story of how the first Tewalas (which he transcribed as “Duwallis”)
               speared a giant dog-salmon and then

                    was dragged out of his canoe and taken down to the dog-salmon’s village
                    under the waters of the Skeena River. . . . After spending two years in the dog-
                    salmon’s village, Duwallis returned to Kitwanga knowing the habits of the
                    dog-salmon so well that he could catch them whenever he wished. Thus he
                    became rich and powerful, but he died fighting bravely against the Indians of
                    Kitselas who split him in two.

              In Marius Barbeau’s 1929 version, Tewalas first cures the salmon chief of
            an infirmity:

                    The live salmon, in gratitude, appeared to him as human beings in a canoe, at the
                    river’s edge, and took him to their home down the river. They led him into three
                    huge houses of the Salmon tribe; on the front of one was painted the
                    Dog-Salmon. . . . The salmon in those houses behaved as human beings. When
                    the time for the salmon run arrived the young man was provided with a fish
                    ­garment and, changing into a salmon, he swam up the river with the school of
                     salmon until he reached the canyon, at the edge of which stood his home village.
                     There his uncle Raraotsen caught a gigantic salmon which he could barely drag
                     out of the water. In its body he discovered his nephew, who had disappeared
                     ­several moons before. The Dog-Salmon thereafter became the family crest.

            Barbeau also noted that the Dog-Salmon crest has been represented as a
            naxnox mask in a dramatic performance connected with the assumption of
            chiefly status.35

            return. The towers topped with gold balls (representing rocks to which
            Nuxalk tied their canoes at the time of a great flood), the blue and white
            stripes (representing the snow on the mountain peak), and the dormer win-
            dows (through which peek animals who inhabit the mountain) also recall
            the architecture of northern European houses.
                  Chief Clellamin’s house no longer stands at Quemqte. It was, however,
            replicated from historical photographs and surviving sculptures for the
            ­Canadian Museum of Civilization in the mid-1980s by Nuxalk carver Glenn
             Tallio (b. 1939) and others. On the Northwest Coast, the authenticity of
             such replicas depends not on the physical survival of objects but on the
             ­valorization of remembered images by those who have inherited the rights
              to them. The contemporary house suggests other kinds of historical conver-
              gence. The visit of the Nuxalk to Berlin inspired the young Franz Boas to
              make North American ethnology his life’s work, and his legacy of meticu-
              lous ethnological recording and museum anthropology has facilitated the
              work of contemporary Northwest Coast artists and scholars in their work of
              replication and recovery.
                  It is common to state that the carving of new totem poles, like traditional
              architecture and the painting of crest designs on house fronts, came to an
              end at the end of the nineteenth century. Yet during the middle decades of
              the twentieth century, in Gitwangak and a few other places on the ­Northwest
              Coast, several forces converged to ensure the preservation of some poles
              and their stories: Native determination to defend their traditions against
              assimilationism, the salvage ethnography of museum anthropologists, and
              the government’s desire to promote tourism and economic development.
              When in 1936 a flood of the Skeena River washed away totem poles in a
              number of Gitksan villages, the people set about restoring them. In the mid-
              1940s, potlatches were held in the villages when the poles were raised
              again.36 At the same time, ethnologists at the National Museum of Canada
              collaborated with the Canadian Pacific Railroad to restore and move poles at
              Gitwangak to new places more accessible to tourists. A similar, economi-
              cally motivated restoration project for Alaskan Tlingit poles took place
              during the 1930s under a New Deal program, the Civilian Conservation
              Corps.37 Although most people thought, until recently, that the social and
              political system the poles symbolize was no longer valid, in the early twenty-
              first centuries, the old titles and privileges continue to be passed on and new
              poles are being erected that achieve and surpass the quality of the old ones.
              We recognize today both the different forms that active resistance to
              ­assimilation took during the twentieth century and the ways in which
               ­tourist-oriented ventures could contribute to the survival of historical
                memory in Native communities.38


            The Potlatch
            In addition to the carving of crest poles, powerful Northwest Coast fami-
            lies also display their crests on objects that are visible only on ceremonial
            occasions, such as clothing, dance screens, and masks. The complete set
            of crests belonging to a family will be represented individually, for
            example, on its clan hats, on headdresses known as frontlets, and button

    232      |   T he North w est C oa st




                                  6.22 Tlingit, Juneau, Alaska, Participants wearing button blankets at the opening parade of
                               “Celebration,” 2010. Cloth, thread, mother of pearl buttons. Photo by Janet Catherine Berlo.
                               For the Native people of Southeast Alaska, the festivities that take place every two years
                               provide an opportunity to express their joy in their traditions. Several thousand people take
                               part in a ceremonial march through the state’s capitol, wearing some version of their families’
                               crests on their clothing.



                               blankets (fig. 6.22). The most important occasion for such displays is the
                               potlatch (fig. 1.28). Potlatches include feasts at which rights to the inheri-
                               tance of wealth and power are displayed and validated. A great family shows
                               its worthiness to inherit and hold titles by lavish feasting, by generous dis-
                               tributions of gifts to guests, and by exhibiting its crests while dramatically
                               reenacting or telling their stories. The precise occasions for holding a
                               ­potlatch vary from one people to another. Among the Kwakwaka’wakw, for
                                example, potlatches are occasions, in the words of ­        Kwakwaka’wakw
                                ­anthropologist and curator Gloria Cranmer Webster, for “naming children,
                                 mourning the dead, transferring rights and privileges, and, less frequently,
                                 marriages or the raising of memorial totem poles.”39
                                    The Kwakwaka’wakw potlatch has been much celebrated because it fea-
                                 tures some of the most dramatic and theatrically sophisticated masked per-
                                 formances to be found on the Northwest Coast. It was very well ­documented
                                 at the turn of the twentieth century, furthermore, in the ethnographic ac-
                                 counts and collections made by Franz Boas and his associate, George Hunt




06-Berlo-Chap06.indd 232                                                                                                     22/05/14 5:13 PM
                                      C o nt e x t s f o r A r t : Po w e r, St at u s , a n d C r o s s - c u lt u r a l E x c h a n g e   |   233


            (1854–1933), son of a Tlingit mother and a Hudson Bay ­Company em-
            ployee, who was raised among the Kwakwaka’wakw. Tradition has it that
            the Kwakwaka’wakw acquired a number of masks and dances from the
            Heiltsuk to the north, but the creation of an unparalleled array of visual
            forms and dramatic techniques with which to display these dance privileges
            was a local development. Boas and Hunt’s collections include a wealth of
            carved masks, puppets, props, and dance screens used to tell crest stories
            and to initiate high-ranking people into the Hamatsa and other elite danc-
            ing societies. In masquerades the themes of spirit possession, transforma-
            tion, and the domestication of power acquired from the spirit world are
            given a new temporal and spatial reality, adding further kinetic and dra-
            matic dimensions to the painterly and sculptural techniques of representa-
            tion ­a lready described. The highly realistic dramas included events in which
            (by prearrangement) masked beings appeared to draw blood and cut bits of
            flesh from audience members in the graphic display of their dangerous
            powers, and others in which people were apparently dismembered before
            the eyes of the spectators, only to return reassembled. Magical transforma-
            tions from animal to human were made vivid by transformation masks,
            constructed with hidden strings manipulated by the masker (fig. 6.10).
                Initiation into the elite Hamat’sa society is a featured element of pot-
            latches held at the time of the Tseka cycle, the first of the two ceremonial
            cycles of the Kwakwaka’wakw winter ceremonial season. As we have already
            seen in the context of Straits Salish shamanism, winter is a time when the
            presence of supernatural beings is more apparent in the villages, and the
            Kwakwakw’wakw ceremonials thus illustrate the general Northwest Coast
            seasonal pattern. A century ago, the first sign that the Tseka winter cycle
            was to occur was the disappearance from the village of the high-born young
            men who had inherited the privilege of Hamat’sa membership. They were
            said to have been captured by the man-eating spirits who live in the far
            north with their leader Baxwbakwalanuxwsiwe. Their return as initiates,
            ­endowed with new powers, is still the highlight of the Tseka cycle. The com-
             panions of Baxwbakwalanuxwsiwe are impersonated by maskers wearing
             giant headpieces representing up to four different species of man-eating
             birds (fig. 6.23, center foreground). Their masks have great snapping beaks
             and they dance to display and purge the destructive power the initiates have
             acquired during their absence. Boas describes the Hamat’sa initiate moving
             among the spectators, biting and drawing blood (although this no longer
             occurs). It is the role of the women of the society to tame and control the
             initiates, a process expressed in the slow, potent movements of the dance,
             so that the initiates’ new powers become socially constructive rather than
             destructive. The singers and audience wear head rings made of shredded red
             cedar bark, symbolizing the Tseka season, and carrying significations of the
             human realm and social order. By the end of the initiation the new mem-
             bers, too, have exchanged their wild hemlock branches for cedar bark rings.
             Although some of the other dances described by Boas have not been per-
             formed for many years, the Hamat’sa performance remains a vital part of
             Kwakwaka’wakw ceremonial life. As Aaron Glass has shown, during the
             twentieth century—in part through Boas’s work and through a famous

                                       At the heart of central and northern Northwest Coast potlatches is a series
                                    of great wealth givers, supernaturals who are capable of bestowing on those
                                    who succeed in besting them extraordinary treasures of copper, dances, food,
                                    and goods of all kinds. They tend to appear, in particular, at potlatches held
                                    for funerals and marriages, because these are prime occasions for the transfer
                                    of wealth. The Gonak’Adet of the Tsimshian and Haida is one such wealth
                                    giver, a fabulous being that lives under the water and controls the salmon.
                                    Among the Kwakwaka’wakw peoples, the wealth giver par excellence is the
                                    Dzunuk’wa, a hairy and wild cannibalistic woman who lives in the woods and
                                    wanders around seeking children to eat, a pack basket on her back to hold her
                                    prey. The mask that represents her is black, with hollowed-out cheeks, bear-
                                    skin eyebrows, empty holes for eyes, and thick pursed lips through which her
                                    impersonator emits the Dzunuk’wa’s characteristic howling sound. Yet
                                    Dzunuk’wa, too, is a source of treasure, especially copper. Her identity as a
                                    source of good things is expressed metaphorically by huge feast dishes carved
                                    in her image (fig. 6.24). Among Coast Salish the swaixwe is also a giver of
                                    wealth, although it is not, like the other two, a chiefly prerogative but an in-
                                    herited privilege whose dance is a purification ritual that cleanses a place of
                                    bad spirits (fig. 6.25).
                                       During the middle and second half of the nineteenth century, as ­permanent
                                    white settlement of the Northwest Coast expanded, competing religious and
                                    political systems increased the pressure on the traditional ­institutions of
                                    Northwest Coast life and art. Missionaries as well as government officials

                                        C o nt e x t s f o r A r t : Po w e r, St at u s , a n d C r o s s - c u lt u r a l E x c h a n g e   |   235


            mounted direct attacks on the potlatch because Victorian ­society disapproved
            of the magnificent displays and (apparent) wasting of wealth that was re-
            quired to maintain the prestige of great families. The banning of the potlatch
            in the 1885 Canadian Indian Act thus threatened the survival of Indigenous
            systems of political authority, oral history, and traditional art. It was not until
            1951 that this ban was dropped. Despite the repressive policies that remained
            in force during the first half of the twentieth century, many Northwest Coast
            peoples found ways to continue potlatching. Yet by the early 1900s, it ap-
            peared both to non-Natives and also to many Aboriginal people that the
            richly expressive system that had developed on the Northwest Coast over
            many millennia was rapidly coming to an end. During the second half of the
            twentieth century, however, Northwest Coast people reversed this history in
            a remarkable reassertion of cultural and artistic energy.

            Art, Commodity, and Oral Tradition
            The history of Haida art illustrates with particular starkness the threat posed
            to traditional artistic heritages during the second half of the nineteenth
            century. Yet it also demonstrates the important role that commodified pro-
            ductions of curios and souvenirs have played in maintaining fragile links to
            ancient artistic heritages. In their own right, furthermore, the new artistic
            possibilities presented by art commodities have stimulated much innovation
            and creativity.

                                        After the 1860s, however, when the normal outlets for the visual represen-
                                     tation of crest stories and other traditional images were closed off, the imag-
                                     ery of argillite carvings began to change further. Haida carvers continued to
                                     carve elaborate plates, platters, and candlesticks that imitate the contours of
                                     European china and metalwork, but they began to add figures from tradi-
                                     tional Haida stories, many of which had not previously been ­depicted in a
                                     fully narrative manner. The popular story of the Bear Mother, for example,
                                     which tells of a woman kidnapped by a supernatural bear who bore twin half-
                                     bear children, is associated with a crest belonging to ­Tsimshian families. The
                                     story is represented on totem poles as a single figure, usually of a bear with
                                     some human attributes. Depictions of the story in argillite are much more
                                     explicit and expressive; in one figure the Bear Mother’s pain as she nurses her
                                     half-bear children is vividly shown in the expression on her face.43 Carvers
                                     also used argillite to make miniatures of totem poles and other ceremonial
                                     objects they could no longer carve at full size. These were avidly collected by
                                     the tourists who stopped at Haida Gwaii on the newly popular boat trips, but
                                     they also served important needs of the Haida themselves, keeping tradi-
                                     tional stories and art styles alive. Indeed, one of the greatest carvers of the
                                     Victorian period, Charles ­Edenshaw, made some of his finest works in argil-
                                     lite (fig. 6.26). The legacy he and other late nineteenth-century artists left
                                     proved critical to the twentieth-century revival of Haida art.

               ARTISTS IN FOCUS
               Charles and Isabella Edenshaw

               In 1885 a traditional marriage was celebrated at the Haida
               village of Massett between Qwii.aang and Da.a xiigang.
               After a second, Anglican ceremony, they became known as
               Isabella and Charles Edenshaw, two of the most famous
               names in the history of Northwest Coast art. Isabella
               (1858–1926) was an expert weaver of hats, baskets, and
               mats; Charles (1839–1920) painted flowing crest designs
               on his wife’s hats and produced a corpus of works in
               ­argillite, wood, and silver that remain consummate exam-
                ples of classic Haida art.

                illustrate the new relationships between traditional and

          Isabella and Charles’s children, grandchildren, and great-
      grandchildren have continued the family tradition of artistic
      excellence and innovation. Their great-nephew Bill Reid
      (fig. 6.1 and chapter 7) began his career by studying Charles
      Edenshaw’s silver bracelets and other artworks and records
      preserved in museums. Reid, in turn, helped train Robert
      Davidson, the Edenshaws’ great grandson (fig. 7.24). When
      in 2011 Jim Hart (b. 1952), another great-grandson and the
      current holder of the title Chief Idensu [Edenshaw], was com-
      missioned to create a monumental bronze statue of tradi-
      tional Haida guardian figures outside the National Gallery of
      Canada in Ottawa, the Edenshaw legacy gained a monumen-
      tal public presence that could not have been imagined in
      1900 (fig. 6.28).

                                      also used his drawings to illustrate his classic book Primitive Art. The artist
                                      also accepted commissions from Boas, Swanton, and others to make models
                                      of the totem poles, traditional houses, and other large sculptures that were
                                      disappearing and could no longer be replaced. Taken together, his artistic
                                      commissions and his collaborations with leading anthropologists of his day

                                      also to attribute works made by other artists and understand the imagery

                                      Northwest Coast Art Since the Beginning
                                      of the Twentieth Century
                                      During the first half of the twentieth century, some Northwest Coast artists
                                      continued to make traditional art for use in potlatches. They and others also
                                      used traditional imagery to make model totem poles and other miniatures
                                      for the souvenir trade. The model poles and innovative silk-screened scarves
                                      made by Ellen Neel (Kwakwaka’wakw, 1916–66) heralded the taking up of




06-Berlo-Chap06.indd 238                                                                                           22/05/14 5:13 PM
                                 No r t h w e s t C o a s t A r t S i n c e t h e B e g i n n i n g o f t h e Tw e nt i e t h C e nt u r y   |   239


            traditionally male art forms by women artists. Throughout this period, as
            we have seen, museums continued to collect crest poles, many of which had
            fallen and were being allowed to decay. By the late 1940s, some poles that
            had been placed outdoors at the University of British Columbia were show-
            ing such evidence of weathering that the curator of the University’s Museum
            of Anthropology, Audrey Hawthorn, engaged Mungo Martin (1879–1962), a
            Kwakwaka’wakw carver and one of the few living artists trained in the tra-
            ditional apprenticeship system, to come to Vancouver and undertake their
            restoration. This project soon led to commissions for new carvings, and, in
            the 1950s, to further projects of similar kinds at the British Columbia
            Provincial Museum in Victoria. Martin took as apprentices Henry Hunt,
            Tony Hunt, and Douglas Cranmer, and initiated the training of a new gen-
            eration of Northwest Coast carvers. He also collaborated with Bill Reid, who,
            born and raised in Victoria, had been a radio announcer by profession and
            had also trained as a maker and designer of modern jewelry. (His work will
            be discussed further in chapter 7.)
                 With these events and in the climate of liberalism, antiracist activism,
            and movements of national liberation that characterized the 1960s, a new
            era of art-making opened on the Northwest Coast, an era in which many
            traditional forms have been made again and others reinvented to fill the
            gaps in memory and use created by colonial repression. The vital link
            ­between ritual celebration and art was also reasserted in these years. The
             potlatch organized in 1953 by Mungo Martin to inaugurate the newly
             ­completed big house that he and his apprentices had built for the British
              Columbia Provincial Museum (now the Royal British Columbia Museum)
              was the first to be held openly since the ban imposed by the 1885 law and
              signaled the end of official repression. The new era saw not only a renewal of
              the carving of traditional architectural sculpture and masks but also the
              emergence of new genres like printmaking and free standing public sculp-
              tures such as The Raven and the First Men (fig. 6.1). Carvers have worked for
              both Native and non-Native patrons carving masks that continue to display
              inherited family privileges at potlatches, as well as others that are collected
              and marketed as “fine art” by urban art galleries.
                 In 1970 the Kitanmax School of Northwest Coast Indian Art was estab-
              lished as part of K’san Historic Indian Village in the territories of the
              Gitk’san, at Hazelton, British Columbia. Artists who had worked on the
              Vancouver and Victoria museum projects came to teach, together with
              others who had been pursuing similar projects. ‘Ksan was important not
              only in disseminating the skills honed by the pioneering generation of
              Kwakwaka’wakw and Haida artists but also in stimulating the renewal of
              local art traditions. Nuu-chah-nulth artists such as Ki-Ke-In (Ron H­ amilton,
              b. 1948), Art Thompson (1948–2003), and Joe David (b. 1946); Tsimshian
              artists Walter Harris (1931–2009) and Norman Tait (b. 1941); and Coast
              Salish artists such as Stan Greene (b. 1953) and Susan Point (b. 1952) have
              all worked to reestablish the integrity of their own distinctive stylistic and
              iconographic traditions.

                The renewal of artistic traditions all along the Northwest Coast from
            Oregon to Alaska has been the work of countless community members and
            artists. It is a movement that insists that tradition can thrive at the core of
            modern life. Whether carver, jeweler, weaver, or high fashion designer,
            these artists embrace the modern—the topic of the next chapter—as they
            make use of Western genres and media, transgress older gender boundaries
            in the making of art, and participate in art markets while also making
            ­traditional works that equal or even surpass those of their illustrious fore-
             bears. As we will see in the next two chapters, however, in the process of
             renewal contemporary artists also draw on an ethnographic record created
             by outsiders to recover traditions interrupted by numerous forms of colo-
             nial suppression and intervention. The portrait Nicholas Galanin carved out
             of the pages of a major ethnography of his own Tlingit people reminds us
             that colonial histories of representation are inevitably intertwined with
             contemporary cultural expressions (fig. 1.8).

            In 1978, in a studio rented especially to accommodate the huge eight-by-
            twenty-seven-foot canvas, the Anishinaabe painter Daphne Odjig (b. 1919)
            completed what is arguably her masterwork, The Indian in Transition
            (fig. 7.1). Modernist in its flattened space, intertwined curvilinear forms,
            and expressive coloration, it nevertheless deviated from the high modernist
            modes of abstraction that were then current. Rather, it belonged to the
            unfashionable genre of history painting, forcefully recounting Aboriginal
            experiences of precolonial life, colonial oppression, and the dawning of a
            new postcolonial era. As Mohawk curator Lee Ann Martin has written of
            the work:

                    The Indian in Transition takes the viewer on an historical odyssey that
                    begins before the arrival of Europeans, continues through the devastation and
                    destruction of Aboriginal cultures, and ends on an expression of rejuvenation
                    and hope. Odjig’s story unfolds with the figure on the left playing the drum,
                    which symbolizes strong Aboriginal cultural traditions, while overhead is a
                    protective Thunderbird. Then a boat arrives filled with pale-skinned people.
                    The boat’s bow becomes a serpent, a bad omen in Anishnabe mythology.
                       Next, Odjig depicts Aboriginal people trapped in a vortex of political,
                    social, economic, and cultural change. Four ethereal figures rise above the

                                    When Odjig’s masterwork was first unveiled, the art world did not know
                                 how to categorize it. In addition to its insistence on narrative and figural
                                 representation, it was made by a self-taught artist inspired by earlier
                                 twentieth-century modernist works such as Picasso’s 1937 Guernica rather
                                 than by the issues of abstract pictorial form and space being addressed by
                                 leading painters in the 1970s. It drew on Aboriginal traditions of storytell-
                                 ing, explored the capacity of visual art to give expression to Indigenous
                                 historical memory, and advanced a strong political and social agenda. Odjig’s
                                 ability to make art that served these purposes was the result of a history of
                                 Native North American artists’ experiences of modernity and negotiations
                                 of Western artistic modernism that we explore in this chapter.


                                 The Multiplicity of Modernisms
                                 There are as many modes of modern Native North American art as there are
                                 Native ways of living in modernity. Yet numerous confusions cloud the
                                 question of which artists and art forms should be considered in this chap-
                                 ter. Must a work be produced in Western fine art media and formats, or
                                 should we include all forms of art made by Native people during the period
                                 of Western modernism, including those we designate as “craft”? If artists
                                 adopt Western media, must they deal with current issues, or should works
                                 that address traditional heritage be included? Are professional art school
                                 training and familiarity with contemporary avant-garde idioms prerequi-
                                 sites, or are apprenticeship and the use of historical styles sufficient?

                                 Problems of Definition: Indigenous, Modern, Modernist
                                 The fundamental problems of identity discussed in chapter 1 further com-
                                 plicate this issue. To be judged “Native,” must the work be made by an artist
                                 whose Native status is legally recognized by the U.S. or Canadian govern-
                                 ment? Changes in U.S. and Canadian laws during the late 1980s and early
                                 1990s resulted in the sudden bestowal or withdrawal of legal recognition as
                                 “Indian” for a number of artists who have contributed in important ways to
                                 the development of modern and contemporary Native North American art
                                 (see chapter 1, pp. 27–28). In this chapter and the next we discuss work by
                                 artists of Native or part-Native ancestry whose artistic concerns have been
                                 formed by their identification with Native communities. The artist’s subjec-
                                 tivity rather than bureaucratic or legislated definitions is, thus, the primary
                                 criterion for inclusion. For example, architect Douglas Cardinal’s (fig. 1.11)
                                 identification with his Blackfoot heritage has been lifelong, although his
                                 legal Aboriginal status was only restored after the 1983 change in Canadian
                                 law discussed in chapter 1. Modernist painter Fritz Scholder began his
                                 career determined not to be an “Indian artist,” but, as we will see, he revolu-
                                 tionized the orientation of contemporary Aboriginal art as a mature artist
                                 (fig. 7.27). Installation artist Alan Michaelson’s formation was different yet
                                 again; he was adopted out of his Haudeosaunee reserve and reconnected
                                 with his heritage and community as an adult (fig. 8.25).
                                    We also need to explain a key distinction we make between “modern”
                                 and “modernist” arts. To do this, it will be useful first to clarify three




07-Berlo-Chap07.indd 244                                                                                      23/05/14 12:08 PM
                                                                        T h e Mu lt i p l i c it y o f Mo d e r n i s m s    |   24 5


            interrelated terms that can be easily confused: “modernity,” “moderniza-
            tion,” and “modernism.” We understand “modernity” to be a period defined
            by social, political, and economic changes that began in the eighteenth cen-
            tury. “Modernization” refers to the processes, systems, and ideologies that
            produce modernity, primary among which are industrialization, urbaniza-
            tion, capitalism, colonialism, nationalism, and secularism. “Modernism”
            describes a range of cultural inventions through which people express
            their experiences of living in modernity. Marshall Berman, one of the most
            influential theorists of modernity, has urged such distinctions in an evoca-
            tive and compelling way. “To be modern,” he writes, “is to experience
            personal and social life as a maelstrom, to find one’s world and oneself in
            perpetual disintegration and renewal, trouble and anguish, ambiguity and
            contradiction: to be part of a universe in which all that is solid melts into
            air. To be a modernist is to make oneself somehow at home in the mael-
            strom, to make its rhythms one’s own, to move within its currents in search
            of the forms of reality, of beauty, of freedom, of justice, that its fervid and
            perilous flow allows.”2
               Berman also strongly affirms the global nature of modernity: “In the
            twentieth century,” he writes, “the process of modernization expands to
            take in virtually the whole world, and the developing world culture of mod-
            ernism achieves spectacular triumphs in art and thought.”3 As seen repeat-
            edly in this book, the Indigenous peoples of North America, like other
            colonized peoples, have lived in modernity and actively participated in mod-
            ernization from its earliest phases. Indeed, if the “maelstrom” of “disinte-
            gration and renewal, trouble and anguish, ambiguity and contradiction” are
            its markers, Native North Americans have experienced modernity in par-
            ticularly intense and precocious forms for hundreds of years. Yet colonial
            policies prevented most from engaging in modernist artistic practices until
            the second half of the twentieth century. Rather, during this century, art-
            ists have expressed their experiences of modernity in a wide range of styles
            and genres, some of which we define as “modern” and others as “modernist.”
            By adopting this more inclusive approach, we recognize the authenticity of
            each art form in relation to its individual context of production.
               We identify as “modern” works made by artists who depart from inher-
            ited traditions of art-making to produce art that self-consciously communi-
            cates with outside audiences through Western traditions of graphic and
            sculptural representation. Thus, when Fred Kabotie earned money by paint-
            ing traditional Pueblo life (fig. 2.14), or when Potawatomi artist Woodie
            Crumbo (1912–89) portrayed tourists gawking at a Navajo woman display-
            ing a rug for sale (fig. 1.20), they were participating in modern forms of art
            production. Their works were made to address both Native and non-Native
            viewers, and they reflect on new economies of art specific to colonized
            peoples living in modernity. Similarly, we include among the modern arts
            twentieth-century Inuit and Alaskan Eskimo carvings, prints, and paint-
            ings which have long been addressed in isolation not only from twentieth-
            century settler arts but also from the contemporary arts of other Native
            North Americans. In the first edition of this book we discussed the work
            of Arctic artists in conjunction with their ancient and historical arts

                                 (see chapter 5). Here we also consider them as productions that exemplify
                                 key aspects of the modern in art—experiences of modernization, the pres-
                                 ervation of historical memory, and participation in outside markets.
                                    “Modernist” works are a subset within the large and diverse panoply of
                                 modern arts. We categorize as “modernist” works produced by artists who
                                 chose to engage with the specific conceptual and stylistic movements in-
                                 vented by twentieth-century Western artists. When Daphne Odjig adopted
                                 cubist principles of spatial representation in her work of the 1970s, or when
                                 George Morrison began to create abstract expressionist paintings during
                                 the late 1940s, both were engaging with specifically modernist styles and
                                 concepts of art-making shared with other Western and non-Western
                                 artists (fig. 7.2).
                                    The decision to work with new technologies of mechanical reproduction is
                                 also a hallmark of the modern. A number of Native artists saw photography,
                                 like painting, as a useful medium that could also be recruited to document
                                 modern Indigenous lives. Horace Poolaw (Kiowa, 1906–84) (fig. 1.18), Peter
                                 Pitseolak (Inuit, 1902–73; fig. 7.16), and Lee Marmon (Laguna Pueblo, b. 1925),
                                 for example, taught themselves to use the camera to record the faces of elders, the
                                 changing landscapes of their communities, and twentieth-century social rituals
                                 that ranged from traditional Eagle Dancers in New Mexico to square dances en-
                                 joyed in a village hall by Inuit and white residents of Cape Dorset. Scholars con-
                                 tinue to uncover other pioneering photographers, such as Haida Benjamin
                                 Haldane (1874–1941) and Cherokee Jennie Ross Cobb (1881–1959).
                                    Self-identification as modern, modernist, and Aboriginal could, as already
                                 noted, modulate over the course of a career. Morrison, for example, chose
                                 modernism and abstraction precisely because, as Bill Anthes has written,
                                 “[he] preferred the universal, modernist identity of the artist as an individ-
                                 ual. Reductive and stereotypical understandings of what constituted Native

                                                                         T h e Mu lt i p l i c it y o f Mo d e r n i s m s    |   2 47


            American art encouraged Morrison to fashion an identity for himself as a
            modernist, whose Indian heritage was unrelated to his work as an artist.”4
            During the 1970s, however, as decolonizing movements gained momentum
            and as minorities fought for respect and recognition of their civil rights and
            unique identities, Morrison responded to the heightened consciousness of
            historical oppression of Native Americans and their struggles for full human
            rights. He participated in the activism and protests of the American Indian
            movement and gave titles to some of his later paintings that explicitly refer-
            ence his identification with his Anishinaabe homelands. Artistic careers
            such as Morrison’s evidence the multiple ways in which modernism could be
            negotiated in relation to individual needs, local histories, and changing
            political contexts. It is important to stress, however, that both modern and
            modernist engagements with Western media, styles, and genres are negotia-
            tions that reinvent, modify, and diverge from Western traditions in order to
            express uniquely Indigenous perspectives and cultural dispositions.


            Primitivism, the “Time Lag,” and Multiple Modernisms
            Most textbooks and museums have narrated the story of modern art in
            terms of a specific sequence of European formal and conceptual innovations
            that began in late nineteenth-century France with Van Gogh, Cezanne,
            Gauguin, and their associates. During the first two decades of the twentieth
            century, European artists made even more radical breaks with previous
            Western modes of visual representation—Picasso’s cubism, Matisse’s color-
            ism and planar compositions, Kandinsky’s abstraction. Modernist artists
            rejected illusionistic space in favor of flatness of surface; they worked re-
            flexively with the component elements of visual art such as space, line,
            color, and form; and—in many cases—they abandoned figuration in favor
            of abstraction and expressionism. They promoted the value of individual
            freedom and self-expression and subscribed to a universalist ideology that
            rejected Western academic and classical traditions in order to promote in-
            stead the creation of a shared visual language that could be comprehended
            across cultural boundaries.
               In pursuit of these goals, the modernists sought inspiration in works of
            so-called primitive art from Africa, Oceania, and the Americas that they
            believed to have remained closer to basic, primordial human truths. The
            engagement with the primitive was so integral to artistic modernism that
            in 1938 Robert Goldwater, the author of an early and still definitive study,
            could affirm that modern art’s “primitivist features may be considered not
            merely accidents, but of its essential nature.”5 Analysts of the still pervasive
            taste for “primitive art” have demonstrated its falsity as a category. The idea
            of primitive art was invented by Europeans to comfort themselves for the
            cultural losses produced by modernization. As discussed later in this
            chapter, for example, the non-Inuit artists who first promoted Inuit sculp-
            ture in the mid-twentieth century appreciated the work of a carver such as
            John Pangnark because the economical and simplified forms of his figures
            seemed to them to reveal powerful and elemental truths and a strong affin-
            ity with their own aesthetic taste for anticlassical and radically simplified
            forms (see fig. 7.21).




07-Berlo-Chap07.indd 247                                                                                                     23/05/14 12:08 PM
    24 8     |   N ati v e A rt f rom 19 0 0 to 19 8 0 : Mode rn s and Mode rni s t s


                                    The term “primitive” is thus more revealing of European than of non-
                                 Western cultures and worldviews. When we use the terms “primitivism” or
                                 “primitive art” in this book, we are referring to an historical movement
                                 within art history that is still unfolding and not to imply agreement with
                                 the idea that some arts are more primitive than others. Rather, the modern-
                                 ists’ love of primitive art harbored fundamental contradictions. As dis-
                                 cussed in chapter 1, the objects they most admired were old pieces that
                                 seemed to show little or no Western influence. (Often, they were mistaken,
                                 and the works they admired were in fact produced within the condition of
                                 modernity as we have just defined it.) For all these reasons, when the
                                 modern Indigenous arts of Native North Americans came to the notice
                                 of non-Native modernist artists and art lovers, they tended either to em-
                                 brace them as the last traces of ancient ways of life or to dismiss them as
                                 inauthentic.
                                    One reason for these judgments was the time lag between the initial
                                 period of modernist innovation in Europe and Native North American art-
                                 ists’ engagements with modernist styles and concepts. This lag resulted, on
                                 the one hand, from the geographic isolation imposed during the reservation
                                 era, during which most Indigenous North Americans were confined to lands
                                 distant from the urban environments where modernist arts flourished.
                                 On the other hand, it was a product of the limited “industrial” curricula of
                                 the Indian boarding and residential schools, which did not prepare students
                                 to enter professional art schools where the new styles were disseminated.
                                 The time lag between the emergence of modernist Aboriginal art in the mid-
                                 twentieth century and the modernisms invented in France and continental
                                 Europe in the early 1900s made non-Western modern arts seem derivative
                                 and provincial. With some exceptions, those museums that did acquire
                                 twentieth-century Aboriginal paintings and sculptures valued them as
                                 ethnographic documentation of traditional beliefs and lifestyles. In conse-
                                 quence, Aboriginal arts, whether modern or modernist, have been largely
                                 excluded from art history surveys and museum installations of twentieth-
                                 century art. In the twenty-first century, however, accounts of modernism’s
                                 history have begun to change. In keeping with current approaches to
                                 African, Asian, and other world modernisms, we argue here that the modern
                                 period in art is comprised not of a single unified Euro-American history, but
                                 of multiple histories that unfolded around the world at different moments
                                 in the course of the twentieth century.
                                    Art historian J. J. Brody has succinctly summarized the central contra-
                                 diction that has worked against the acceptance of multiple modernisms:
                                 “Modernism was a historical attitude supporting the ahistorical belief in
                                 the indivisibility of form and content, the union of subject and object, and,
                                 for two-dimensional objects, the tyranny of the picture plane.”6 Postmod-
                                 ernism and globalization, two intellectual and geopolitical developments
                                 that, as further discussed in chapter 8, began to gather momentum during
                                 the last decades of the twentieth century, have disrupted the standard
                                 accounts of modernism as a singular, linear, and progressive development
                                 that took place in Europe and the United States. Western artistic modern-
                                 ism now appears as a specific historical period, like the Renaissance or the




07-Berlo-Chap07.indd 248                                                                                    23/05/14 12:08 PM
                                                                        T h e Mu lt i p l i c it y o f Mo d e r n i s m s    |   249


            Baroque.7 It interacted with the modern visual arts of peoples around the
            world, each of which mediated local art traditions, cultural and political con-
            texts, and—often—colonial histories. Indigenous North American modern
            arts are, in other words, new, original, and reflexive in their own terms.
            Such an approach not only demonstrates modernism’s fertility and avail-
            ability for reinvention but also helps to realize a “world art history” capable
            of representing multiple cultural histories and aesthetic systems.
               Despite the obstacles we have outlined, a small number of aspiring
            artists scattered across the United States and Canada discovered an exciting
            potential in modern art’s universalist ideals and affirmation of a category of
            primitive art that included their own ancestral arts. Adopting modern and
            modernist ways of making art, they could express Indigenous identities,
            cultural traditions, and historical memory at a critical moment in their his-
            tory when their survival and preservation were threatened by the intensifi-
            cation of pressures to assimilate. George Morrison was one of these pioneers.
            Another was the Abenaki abstract painter Rita Letendre (b. 1928). The ar-
            tistic philosophy she articulated as she looked back on her career—“You
            have to discover who you are, then be yourself, no matter what”8 —testifies
            to the compelling and liberating force of the modernist aesthetics and ide-
            ologies she first encountered as a young artist in Montreal during the 1950s.
            For Letendre, “being herself” led her first to reject the conservative aca-
            demic training she was offered as a student at the École des Beaux Arts in
            favor of the surrealism of the new Automatiste movement. She subsequently
            adopted the hard-edge abstraction that dominated the North American art
            world during the 1960s and 1970s, and later mediated that movement’s ex-
            clusive concern with formal problems through titles that reference her long-
            standing interest in the dualities of atmosphere and light, night and day—as
            well as her Abenaki heritage (fig. 7.3).
